name: Attention and Transformers
intent: Understand how a transformer lets every token look at the others and mix in what matters, and why that costs more the longer the text gets.
scenario: In 'The trophy did not fit in the suitcase because it was too big', a reader knows that 'it' means the trophy. A model has to link 'it' to the right word, using only numbers.
problem: A word means different things in different sentences, so a model cannot give each word one fixed vector and stop there. It needs a way for each token to pull in information from the other tokens that matter for it, and to decide which ones matter. Older designs passed information along one step at a time. The transformer does it in one operation that looks at all pairs of tokens at once, which is fast to run on a GPU but grows quickly with the length of the text.

howItWorks.title: Tokens become vectors, with a position
howItWorks.text: Each token ID is looked up as a vector. Attention on its own does not know the order of the tokens, so position information is added to each vector. The original paper used fixed sine and cosine patterns, and many later models use other schemes.

howItWorks.title: Each token makes a query, a key and a value
howItWorks.text: Three different learned projections of a token's vector give its query (what it is looking for), its key (what it offers to others) and its value (what it passes on if it is chosen).

howItWorks.title: Score every pair
howItWorks.text: The score between two tokens is the dot product of one token's query with the other's key, divided by the square root of the key size. The paper scales the scores because large dot products push the softmax into regions where its gradients are very small.

howItWorks.title: Softmax, then mix the values
howItWorks.text: A softmax turns each token's scores into weights that add up to 1. The token's new vector is the weighted sum of the value vectors. 'It' gets a high weight on 'trophy' and a low one on 'the', so it pulls in the meaning of 'trophy'.

howItWorks.title: A mask keeps the future out
howItWorks.text: A model that writes text from left to right may only look at earlier tokens. A causal mask removes the scores for later positions. This is also why the keys and values of earlier tokens never change while new tokens are added, which is what a KV cache relies on.

howItWorks.title: Heads, layers and the cost
howItWorks.text: Several attention heads run side by side, each on a narrower slice of the vector, so the model can attend to different relations at once. A layer adds a feed-forward network and residual connections, and a model stacks many layers. The score matrix has one entry for every pair of tokens, so the work grows with the square of the text length.

pros: Every token can use information from every earlier token in one step, however far apart they are
The pairs can be computed in parallel, which suits GPUs
The weights show which tokens a position used, which helps with inspection
The same block repeated in many layers scales to very large models
cons: The score matrix grows with the square of the sequence length, so very long contexts are expensive
Every token must be kept available (the KV cache), so memory grows with the text length
Attention weights are a clue to what the model used, not a full explanation of its answer
The model has no built-in order, so position information must be added and handled with care
whenToUse: You need to understand why prompt length affects latency and memory
You are reasoning about context windows, long documents or the cost of long prompts
You are reading a model description and need to know what its heads, layers and widths mean
whenNotToUse: Do not treat the attention weights of one layer as an explanation of why the model answered as it did
Do not assume that a longer window means the model uses all of it equally well
Do not expect the mechanism to give the model facts it was never trained on or given
pitfalls: Saying that attention cost is linear in length: the score matrix is quadratic, even if optimised kernels avoid storing it in full
Mixing up the width of the model with the size of one head: with more heads each head is narrower
Forgetting that the key and value vectors of every earlier token must stay in memory while generating
Reading the pattern of a single head as a rule: heads differ and many do not have a clear meaning

roles.label: Token vectors
roles.description: One vector per token, with position information added.

roles.label: Queries and keys
roles.description: Each token's query is compared with the keys of the others to produce scores.

roles.label: Weights and values
roles.description: Softmax turns scores into weights, and each token takes a weighted mix of the value vectors.

roles.label: Layer
roles.description: Attention heads plus a feed-forward block, repeated many times.

quiz.question: A prompt is doubled in length, from 4,000 to 8,000 tokens. Roughly how does the number of attention scores in each layer change?
options: It doubles, because there are twice as many tokens to look at
It stays the same, because attention is computed once for the whole text
It grows about four times, because every token is scored against every other token
It grows about eight times, because the number of heads must double as well
quiz.explanation: The score matrix has one entry for each pair of tokens, so the number of entries grows with the square of the length: twice the tokens gives about four times the pairs. It does not stay fixed, and the number of heads does not need to change.

quiz.question: A language model that writes text from left to right is trained with a causal mask. What would go wrong during training without the mask?
options: Each token could look at the tokens after it, including the very word it must predict, so the model would learn to copy instead of predict
The scores would no longer add up to 1, so the softmax step would fail at training time
The queries and the keys would end up with different sizes, which the dot product cannot handle
The position information would be lost, so the model would not know which token came first
quiz.explanation: Training predicts the next token for every position at once. Without the mask a position could see the answer in the tokens to its right and would learn to copy it, which fails when generating. The softmax, the sizes and the position information are not affected by the mask.

quiz.question: A team changes a model from 8 attention heads to 32, keeping the model width the same. What happens to the size of the score matrices and to the multiply-adds spent on scores in one layer?
options: The cost drops to a quarter, because each head only looks at a quarter of the tokens
The cost grows four times, because there are four times as many score matrices to compute
Each head's slice becomes narrower, so the total multiply-adds for the scores in a layer stay about the same
The cost depends only on the number of layers, so changing the number of heads has no effect on memory
quiz.explanation: With the width fixed, more heads means each head works on a narrower slice of the vector. There are more score matrices, but each multiplication is smaller, so the total multiply-adds for the scores stay about n x n x width. The memory for score matrices does grow with the number of heads, if all are stored.
